cards.title: Draft and edit long-form content in an editable AI canvas
cards.summary: Use an AI assistant that renders the draft in an editable document so you can refine sections, then paste cleanly into your CMS.
cards.use_when: Producing a long-form blog post or category guide for your store and you want an iterative editing loop rather than copy-pasting from chat.
steps: Feed the AI your outline (headings, quick capsule answers, one or two comparison tables, and an FAQ block at the bottom) before asking for a draft.
Ask for the first draft; then edit directly inside the canvas view and also manually where needed, so you get a back-and-forth collaborative pass instead of a one-shot output.
Inject your own first-hand experience into the sections where it matters (e.g., the friction you hit when applying for a city permit), because that detail is what differentiates the content.
Have it flag internal links to relevant pages; since it can't know a non-real site's links, insert the actual internal link targets yourself.
Check that the draft followed your capsule technique and that it cites high-quality sources with working links (e.g., a city permit guide that actually opens).
Paste the finished piece into WordPress and fix the title duplication and any formatting gaps before publishing.
caveats: The specific AI product name and canvas/edit features change over time; verify the current interface before relying on a particular button.
A first draft is 'probably not' ready to publish — expect an experience-injection and sourcing pass.

cards.title: Limit AI-generated question lists to keep content focused
cards.summary: If the model proposes too many sub-questions, cap them so the page stays tight and useful rather than bloated.
cards.use_when: Generating FAQ or Q&A sections for a store guide or informational landing page and the model returns an excessive question list.
steps: Let the model propose questions and headings, but judge whether the total is too long.
Trim the list to the questions your shoppers actually ask; keep the structure you're happy with (headings, brief capsule, one or two tables, bottom FAQ).
Once the structure is approved, request the first draft.
Add more of your own non-public information where you have it, since the more unique detail you place in the prompt, the better the output.
caveats: There is no fixed number of questions that is correct; the limit depends on the topic and page type.

cards.title: Add illustrations to break up text-heavy content (with ecommerce application)
cards.summary: Turn key passages into simple illustrations using a free text-to-visual tool, then convert and place them for impact.
cards.use_when: A product-education section, buying guide, or PDP long-description block reads as a wall of text and you want to make a specific point pop.
steps: Copy just the passage you want to illustrate (e.g., 'how much will an EV charger increase my bill').
In a free text-to-visual tool (the source uses Napkin; a free account has enough capacity), paste the text and generate visuals.
Review the recommended visual, swap it if you don't like it, and pick a styling that fits your site; you can edit elements before exporting.
Export the image and then convert it out of PNG to WEBP (a free PNG-to-WEBP converter works) to keep it light.
Place the WEBP into an image block where it makes sense.
Use this once or twice per post — don't let the page look like nothing but illustrations.
caveats: Don't upload PNGs by default — AI image/visual tools output PNG and heavy images slow the site.
The source did not cover image SEO in detail; treat image-file optimization as the takeaway, not a full image-SEO guide.

cards.title: Write meta descriptions with an AI assist and length target
cards.summary: Have the AI draft the meta description at under ~150 characters to support click-through, then paste into your SEO plugin.
cards.use_when: Finishing a store blog post or category page and you need the title tag and meta description fields filled before publishing.
steps: Confirm whether the AI already produced the meta description; if not, prompt it: 'give me the meta description for this blog post, less than 150 characters.'
Paste the result into the meta description field of your SEO plugin (e.g., Yoast or similar — installing one is recommended but not strictly necessary).
Check the title tag contains the main target keywords.
Review the description for length; the source notes a slightly-too-long description is a common fix-on-sight issue.
caveats: The source states the meta description 'isn't going to make an enormous difference' but can increase CTR — treat it as a CTR nudge, not a ranking lever.

cards.title: Map the whole site structure before building the store
cards.summary: Generate a CSV-style page map (URL, name, title tag, page type, focus) from prior research so the site is planned, not improvised.
cards.use_when: Planning a new store build or a major site restructure and you want the URL hierarchy and page list defined before writing pages.
steps: Use the keyword research, competitor analysis, and page list you already produced as inputs.
Run a 'build your site structure' prompt inside the project that holds that research (works in ChatGPT or Claude) to output a structured sheet.
Expect columns like URL, service/parent page, name, title tag, page type, and focus.
Lay out service/parent pages and child service pages following the URL structure (e.g., services/EV-charger-installation, then services/EV-charger-installation/lutz-florida).
Review the output with common sense and change what doesn't fit; don't copy it blindly.
Lock this structure in as the map you follow during the build.
caveats: The source stresses consistency over an 'ideal' order — don't agonize over whether the service or location comes first in the slug; just stay consistent.
The sheet is described as intentionally rough, a page map rather than a finished blueprint.

cards.title: Deploy the new store and submit it to search consoles
cards.summary: Connect Google Search Console and submit your sitemap so the launched site can actually be found and indexed.
cards.use_when: Just after launching or relaunching an ecommerce site, when you need it discoverable in organic and AI search.
steps: In Google Search Console, go to 'add property', choose the website option, and enter the full new domain; continue and verify ownership.
Locate your sitemap URL (you can check a competitor's the same way to confirm the pattern).
In Search Console's sitemap section, add the new sitemap URL and submit it.
Confirm the status reads success and note the number of discovered pages — a correctly structured site should show many more than a handful.
Work through a launch checklist on a staging site first, then use it as an ongoing on-site SEO checker after launch.
caveats: A site that nobody can find is 'just wasted pixels' — deployment and submission are not optional.
Specific Search Console menus change; verify current navigation.

cards.title: Audit on-page SEO across five core elements plus speed
cards.summary: Check title tag, meta description, H1, H2s, and schema — plus page speed — using a free browser plugin and Lighthouse.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own newly launched store or a site you're optimizing, and you want a fast on-page pass without deep technical work.
steps: Install a free on-page SEO browser extension (the source uses SEO Wallet) and confirm it's active (a small blue bar appears at the left of the page).
Check the title tag contains your main keyword; it doesn't have to be perfect.
Check the meta description length and tighten if slightly too long.
Open the headings tab and verify the H1 and H2s/H3s reflect your primary and secondary keyword targets.

Open the structured data view and confirm the schema that matches the page — e.g., course schema for a course, FAQ page, organization schema; schema changes per page type and isn't needed on every page, but is needed on money pages.

For speed, open Chrome DevTools (top-right three-dot menu → More tools → Developer tools), select the Lighthouse tab, and analyze page load; aim to push performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO as close to 100 as possible.
caveats: On the source's example site, only performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and agentic browsing were all reported at 100; getting everything to 100 is not the norm.
How deep you go on on-page SEO depends on the site type; this is a quick pass, not a full technical audit.

cards.title: Build purposeful internal links into every content page
cards.summary: Internal links improve crawlability, navigation, and pass authority — so link blog content to service/money pages where it makes sense.
cards.use_when: Publishing evergreen store content (buying guides, how-tos, blog posts) and you want it to feed your commercial pages.
steps: Identify your money pages (e.g., the EV charger installation service page) and the related content posts (e.g., cost, permit, level-two posts).
Wherever it genuinely makes sense, add internal links from those posts to the money page — not always, but as often as it fits.
Aim for three purposes: easier crawling for AI and traditional search engines, easier navigation for users, and passing authority to deeper pages.
Remember that the deeper/more inter-linked pages receive less authority, but linking still helps.

Optionally automate with a WordPress plugin like Link Whisper (uses Google Search Console data and adds internal links on new posts) or a content writer tool that handles internal linking when you supply the knowledge base (pages, tone of voice, offer details).
Don't over-complicate — the source keeps internal linking simple and it has worked for them.
caveats: Plugin behavior and integrations change; verify current capability.
Automated tooling still needs your judgment about which links make sense.

cards.title: Track AI visibility with Search Console and Bing AI performance
cards.summary: Use clicks, impressions, average position, and queries from Search Console, and Bing's AI performance tab for citations.
cards.use_when: Monitoring whether your store is surfacing in AI overviews and chat results, and deciding what to do next month.
steps: In Google Search Console's Performance tab, track total clicks and impressions — impressions typically rise first, then clicks; also watch average position across all ranking keywords.
Expect lower clicks generally as AI search engines absorb some traffic; this is described as the new norm, not automatically an error.

Note that Google Search Console doesn't expose AI citation data in all regions, so use Bing Webmaster Tools: authenticate the site (easy once it's in Google Search Console), and open the 'AI performance' section.
Read total citations, average pages cited, and the queries you're cited for; growth in citations and average cited pages is good.
Optionally use a paid AI-visibility tool for additional coverage: a performance tab (citations by engine), a brand tracker for instant checks, and prompt/keyword tracking.
caveats: The source's visibility-tool data skews to US and English queries; that biases the picture for other markets.
There is no target number for how fast citations should rise; the source says judge month-to-month improvement, not an absolute benchmark.

cards.title: Track brand mentions and cited queries, not just rankings
cards.summary: Mentions across Google AI overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity are tracked as a leading indicator alongside clicks.
cards.use_when: Deciding which AI-visibility signals to watch for your store and whether your brand is being recommended.
steps: Use a brand tracker to see what large language models cite you for (e.g., 'internal linking', 'high-quality links') and pull a total mention count across engines.
Track mentions over time — the source example showed mentions decreasing and flagged it as something to investigate.
Treat brand mentions as important, with the source stating they see more conversions attributable to mentions than other AI metrics.
Optionally track specific prompts and keywords, but avoid over-complicating the dashboard.
caveats: The preference for 'mentions over other metrics' is the presenter's opinion, not an established benchmark.
Visibility-tool data is generally US/English-weighted.

cards.title: Start with free local citations before any backlink strategy
cards.summary: Build local directory listings with consistent NAP as the first, cheapest authority layer for a local store.
cards.use_when: Launching a local store and you need foundational authority before investing in link campaigns.
steps: Ask an AI for all free online business listing directories in your target location (e.g., 'free online listing directories for businesses in Dallas, Texas'), and supply more detail about your business type to get more results.
Expect directories like Next Door Business, Foursquare, and the Better Business Bureau — the source says always get on the BBB.
Create a free account wherever allowed and enter your info, keeping NAP (name, address, phone number) consistent across all listings.

For more than three sites, delegate this or use a trusted paid citation service (the source uses Bright Local's local citation building; roughly $3.20 per citation, with a '$2 per citation' rate only at bulk).
Avoid cheap Fiverr-style '300 local citations for $5' offers — they should be a red flag.
caveats: NAP inconsistency across listings is the main risk the source flags.
Pricing was quoted at recording time and may differ now.
Local citations don't replace a backlinking strategy for competitive national niches.

cards.title: Earn expert citations through reporter-request platforms
cards.summary: Answer journalist/publisher questions on a connectivity platform to earn citations and brand mentions with a backlink.
cards.use_when: You or your store's founder have subject-matter authority and want authentic links without buying them.
steps: Create an account on a platform (the source uses 'Connectivity', formerly Featured.com; it used to be HARO/Help a Reporter-style).
After setup and a few questions, you'll see questions publishers are asking; those listing your profile (connected to LinkedIn) are ones the platform predicts you're well-suited for.
Pick the question you can answer best and answer it as thoroughly as you can, then submit.
The answer goes through review, selection, and publication stages; when published you get cited with a link to your site.
Note results vary: the source reports 5 of 12 pitched were published and used the free tier of about three answers per month.
caveats: This 'only really works' for people with some authority or subject-matter expertise in their field.
Publication is not guaranteed; treat the hit rate as variable, not a benchmark.
Platform name and features change — verify the current interface.

cards.title: Buy backlinks only after free options, and vet quality
cards.summary: If you still can't outrank competitors, buy relevant, high-quality links from vetted agencies — never quantity-focused cheap links.
cards.use_when: After you've built the site correctly, published good content, and gotten indexed — and you still aren't outranking competitors.
steps: Sequence it: do all the free things first (local citations, expert citation platforms) before paying for links.
When you buy, prioritize relevance — links from sites related to your industry. A gaming-tech site linking to an SEO teaching site (absent a relevant article) doesn't make sense.
Get on a call with the link provider to verify what they're doing; if they don't know, you'll waste money on poor-quality links.
Agencies mentioned include Get Me Links and Rhino Rank — the source says they've tried both with solid results but can't name a definitive best.
Treat backlinks as the last layer, not a launch necessity.
caveats: Google states it doesn't condone purchasing backlinks; the source observes it remains a large industry because it works, but this is presented as an open secret, not a recommendation of policy.
Fiverr backlink sellers are specifically flagged as easy to get burned by.
The source has not tried all backlink services.

cards.title: Plan the site before building — ingredients before the dish
cards.summary: Do keyword research, competitor analysis, and page mapping first; a structure planned as you go produces a poor result.
cards.use_when: Starting any ecommerce site build or rebuild and you're tempted to just start adding pages.
steps: Complete keyword research, competitor analysis, and the page list before touching the CMS.
Generate the structured page map as described in the site-structure step — the source says this should be easy if prior steps are done.
Use it as a rough page-level understanding of how each page will look and how URLs nest.
Treat the map as the plan you follow consistently during the build, regardless of the platform (WordPress, Webflow, Wix, Astro, etc.).
Only then move to building, deploying, and submitting.
caveats: This is a rough page map, not a finished design spec.
Skipping the plan is described metaphorically as cooking a dish without getting your ingredients first — the source considers it the most important part of the build.
